documents.unit: Office of the Provost (Provost's Taskforce on Syllabus Policy Guidelines for AI Tools)
documents.title: Chapman Considerations for Syllabus Policy on the Use of AI Generative Tools
tiers: Use Permitted: Some Circumstances or With Explicit Permission
documents.summary: Provost's task force guide helping instructors write an AI syllabus statement. It lets each instructor choose, offers sample statements at three permission levels, and cautions against a blanket ban. It also asks departments to settle penalties and promises a university-wide minimum syllabus statement.
documents.stance_why: The guide says Chapman will 'allow individual instructors to determine their own syllabus statement' and offers samples 'by Permission Level' that 'may be used as-is ... or modified', so it sets no stance itself and hands the decision to instructors with three tiers.

units.why: The guidance states Chapman's institutional course of action: it will 'allow individual instructors to determine their own syllabus statement', which hands the decision to instructors (P04 fits better than P56 because the point is who decides).
units.anchor: allow individual instructors to determine their own syllabus statement
units.policy: Chapman offers guidance through university offices and allows individual instructors to determine their own syllabus statement identifying acceptable use of generative AI within the course context.

units.why: The university plans a university-wide syllabus statement to be added to 'minimum syllabus requirements', which is a requirement that every syllabus carry an AI position (P09).
units.anchor: statement to be added to minimum syllabus requirements
units.policy: Chapman will produce a university-wide syllabus statement on acceptable use of generative AI to be added to minimum syllabus requirements.

units.why: The opening framing says 'it is important to develop a policy statement on AI for your syllabus', recommending that every instructor state a policy (P09).
units.anchor: it is important to develop a policy statement on AI for your syllabus
units.policy: Instructors should develop a policy statement on AI for their syllabus and communicate their position clearly to students.

units.why: Academic freedom is invoked: instructors may 'select your own individual approach that aligns to the institutional mission', so instructors choose the rule within institutional bounds (P04).
units.anchor: Academic freedom allows you, the instructor, to select your own individual approach
units.policy: Academic freedom allows the instructor to select their own individual approach that aligns to the institutional mission and policy statement.

units.why: The AI statement must 'make explicit the responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations' per course or assignment, a requirement to communicate expectations (P09).
units.anchor: makes explicit the responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations
units.policy: The instructor's AI statement makes explicit the responsibility of instructors and students to establish clear expectations for generative AI use within each course and/or assignment.

units.why: The statement must reinforce that generative AI use is 'integrally related to academic integrity' and governed by the Academic Integrity Committee, placing AI misuse under integrity processes (P36).
units.anchor: governed by Chapman’s Academic Integrity Committee
units.policy: The instructor's AI statement reinforces that the use of generative AI in academic coursework is integrally related to academic integrity and will be governed by Chapman's Academic Integrity Committee.

units.why: The institutional preamble recognizes that AI 'presents additional challenges to academic integrity and simultaneously presents stimulating opportunities', a framework statement of principles (P56).
units.anchor: generative AI presents additional challenges to academic integrity and simultaneously presents stimulating opportunities
units.policy: The university recognizes that generative AI presents additional challenges to academic integrity and simultaneously presents stimulating opportunities to educate effectively for the future of learning and work.

units.why: The guide tells faculty to check from a student's view that 'course expectations and grading procedures' are clear; this concerns communicating expectations (P09), not a stance.
units.anchor: Are your course expectations and grading procedures clearly articulated?
units.policy: Instructors should check that their syllabus clearly articulates course expectations and grading procedures.

units.why: Departments should hold 'ongoing conversations' about 'appropriate penalties for unauthorized use of an AI', including first-time versus repeat offenders; it asks departments to set penalties (P37) rather than stating one.
units.anchor: appropriate penalties for unauthorized use of an AI
units.frag_start: It is important that faculty and
units.frag_end: violate policies on the use of AI
units.policy: Faculty and administrators should have ongoing conversations within their department/school about the appropriate penalties for unauthorized use of AI, including the level of penalty for first-time offenders and repeat violators.

units.why: The guide asks instructors to 'have honest and open conversations with your students', which is communicating expectations (P09 closest; no type for classroom discussion of integrity).
units.anchor: It is also important to have honest and open conversations with your students.
units.frag_start: It is also important to have
units.policy: Instructors should have honest and open conversations with their students, including about cheating and plagiarism.

units.why: Quoting Darby, the guide advises talking with students about 'the value of doing the work of learning for themselves instead of outsourcing it to a machine', the rationale that AI shortcuts skill-building practice (P41).
units.anchor: doing the work of learning for themselves instead of outsourcing it to a machine
units.policy: Instructors should talk with students about the value of doing the work of learning for themselves instead of outsourcing it to a machine.

units.why: Same Darby passage: 'coach students on the effective use of AI tools related to classwork' recommends teaching AI use, fitting P44.
units.anchor: coach students on the effective use of AI tools related to classwork
units.policy: Instructors should coach students on the effective use of AI tools related to classwork.

units.why: The MLA position statement affirms that 'writing is an important mode of learning', a rationale for protecting writing as learning (P41).
units.anchor: writing is an important mode of learning
units.policy: Writing is an important mode of learning that facilitates analysis and synthesis of information, retention of knowledge, cognitive development, social connection, and participation in public life.

units.why: The statement says educators' work is to support students 'rather than to surveil, discipline, or punish students', a value against policing; P60 is the closest type though it states a value rather than staff declining to detect.
units.anchor: rather than to surveil, discipline, or punish students
units.frag_start: To this end, we believe the
units.policy: The primary work of educators is to support students' intellectual and social development and to foster exploration and creativity rather than to surveil, discipline, or punish students.

units.why: The guide organizes its samples as 'Sample Syllabus Statements by Permission Level', a named-tier structure (P05).
units.anchor: Sample Syllabus Statements by Permission Level
units.policy: The guide offers sample syllabus statements organized by permission level: broad use permitted within guidelines; use permitted in some circumstances or with explicit permission; and no use permitted.

units.why: The note says the samples 'may be used as-is in your syllabus or modified', a template offer where the instructor adopts or adapts (P04).
units.anchor: may be used as-is in your syllabus or modified
units.policy: The sample statements may be used as-is in a syllabus or modified to suit the needs of the course activities and assessments.

units.why: Sample statement: 'students are solely responsible for the accuracy and authenticity of the material', an accountability rule (P29 over P31 because it assigns responsibility for what is submitted).
units.anchor: students are solely responsible for the accuracy and authenticity of the material
units.policy: Students are solely responsible for the accuracy and authenticity of the material that the chatbot generates in response to their prompt or AI query.

units.why: 'It is the student’s responsibility to verify the accuracy of the information provided' requires verifying AI output (P31).
units.anchor: It is the student’s responsibility to verify the accuracy of the information provided
units.policy: Students must verify the accuracy of the information AI provides and use it in ethical ways that avoid academic integrity issues.

units.why: Students 'should also be aware of the inherent bias' in generative AI responses, which names bias (P53; P31 considered but this sentence is about awareness of bias).
units.anchor: the inherent bias that may be manifested in generative AI responses
units.frag_start: Students should also be aware of
units.policy: Students should be aware of the inherent bias that may be manifested in generative AI responses and think critically as they analyze the information provided.

units.why: 'a student’s use of AI tools must be properly documented and referenced' is a disclosure requirement (P24).
units.anchor: use of AI tools must be properly documented and referenced
units.frag_start: To stay in compliance with university
units.policy: A student's use of AI tools must be properly documented and referenced in the citation style of the chosen discipline.

units.why: 'Brainstorming and refining your ideas' is listed among permitted activities, which is brainstorming (P15).
units.anchor: Brainstorming and refining your ideas.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is permitted for brainstorming and refining your ideas.

units.why: 'Fine-tuning your research questions' is a permitted use that fits exploring and developing ideas (P15).
units.anchor: Fine-tuning your research questions.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is permitted for fine-tuning your research questions.

units.why: 'Finding general information about the topic' is a permitted use that is search/tutor-like understanding (P12).
units.anchor: Finding general information about the topic.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is permitted for finding general information about the topic.

units.why: 'Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts' is permitted writing support, so P18 (prose separate from code).
units.anchor: Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is permitted for drafting an outline to organize your thoughts.

units.why: 'Checking grammar, writing conventions, and/or style' is permitted writing support (P18).
units.anchor: Checking grammar, writing conventions, and/or style.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is permitted for checking grammar, writing conventions, and/or style.

units.why: Under 'is not permitted', composing discussion posts or classroom chat content with AI is barred; AI producing submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: Using the AI tool to compose a response to discussion board prompt
units.frag_start: Using the AI tool to compose
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is not permitted to compose a response to a discussion board prompt or to enter content into a chat in a classroom context.

units.why: 'Completing your specific task for assigned group work' with AI is listed as not permitted, barring AI from doing one's share of submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: Completing your specific task for assigned group work.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is not permitted for completing your specific task for assigned group work.

units.why: 'Writing a draft of a writing assignment' is not permitted, a ban on AI producing the submitted draft (P19).
units.anchor: Writing a draft of a writing assignment.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is not permitted for writing a draft of a writing assignment.

units.why: 'Writing entire sentences, paragraphs, or papers to complete class assignments' is not permitted, a ban on AI producing submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: Writing entire sentences, paragraphs, or papers to complete class assignments.
units.policy: Use of generative AI tools is not permitted for writing entire sentences, paragraphs, or papers to complete class assignments.

units.why: 'please ask me for clarification prior to turning in' tells students unsure about a tool to ask the instructor (P10).
units.anchor: If you have questions about whether a specific AI tool is permitted, please ask me
units.frag_start: If you have questions about whether
units.frag_end: prior to turning in classroom or research assignments
units.policy: Students with questions about whether a specific AI tool is permitted should ask the instructor for clarification prior to turning in classroom or research assignments.

units.why: The instructor 'will ask you in for a conference' if AI was used in unauthorized ways, before any referral to the committee; the conference-first step matches P57.
units.anchor: I will ask you in for a conference
units.policy: If the instructor determines that an assignment has used generative AI tools in unauthorized ways, the instructor will ask the student in for a conference, and repeated offences may be brought before Chapman's Academic Integrity Committee for final arbitration.

units.why: Option 2 says 'Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is thus an important concept to engage with', a professional-skill rationale (P44).
units.anchor: Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is thus an important concept
units.policy: Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important concept to engage with thoughtfully as a student and beyond.

units.why: 'Fact-check all AI outputs. Assume it is wrong unless you cross-check the claims' instructs students to verify output (P31).
units.anchor: Fact-check all AI outputs.
units.policy: Students fact-check all AI outputs and assume them wrong unless claims are cross-checked with reliable sources; they are responsible for any errors or omissions.

units.why: 'the use of AI should be acknowledged ... write a short paragraph to explain which AI tool and how you used it' requires an end-of-assignment disclosure statement (P24).
units.anchor: At the end of your assignment, write a short paragraph to explain which AI tool
units.frag_start: Full disclosure: Like any other tool
units.policy: Students write a short paragraph at the end of the assignment explaining which AI tool they used and how, if applicable.

units.why: 'Include the prompts you used to get the results' requires prompts as part of the disclosure (P25: tool and prompt).
units.anchor: Include the prompts you used to get the results.
units.policy: Students include the prompts they used to get the results when disclosing AI use.

units.why: 'Failure to do so is in violation of academic integrity policies' makes non-disclosure itself the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Failure to do so is in violation of academic integrity policies.
units.policy: Failure to disclose AI use as required is a violation of academic integrity policies.

units.why: 'Brainstorm ideas, draft an outline, clarify thoughts, and/or generate keywords' is an approved use (brainstorming, P15).
units.anchor: Brainstorm ideas, draft an outline, clarify thoughts, and/or generate keywords.
units.policy: Students can use generative AI to brainstorm ideas, draft an outline, clarify thoughts, and/or generate keywords.

units.why: 'Fine-tune, expand, or clarify your research questions' is an approved use of exploring ideas (P15).
units.anchor: Fine-tune, expand, or clarify your research questions.
units.policy: Students can use generative AI to fine-tune, expand, or clarify their research questions.

units.why: 'Check grammar, writing conversions, and style; help you find an expression' is approved writing support (P18).
units.anchor: Check grammar, writing conversions, and style; help you find an expression.
units.policy: Students can use generative AI to check grammar, writing conventions, and style and to help find an expression.

units.why: 'Using an AI-content generator such as ChatGPT to complete an assignment without proper attribution violates academic integrity' classifies unattributed AI use as a violation (P36; P28 is about disclosure consequences but the focus here is misconduct).
units.anchor: violates academic integrity
units.policy: Using an AI-content generator such as ChatGPT to complete an assignment without proper attribution violates academic integrity.

units.why: 'you pledge to affirm that they are your own work, and you attribute the use of any tools and sources' asserts ownership and attribution (P29).
units.anchor: you pledge to affirm that they are your own work
units.policy: By submitting assignments, students pledge to affirm that they are their own work and that they attribute the use of any tools and sources.

units.why: Option 1 says outside assigned circumstances 'you are not permitted from using AI tools to generate content' that ends up in course work, a default restriction with exceptions (P01 since it is the default rule).
units.anchor: you are not permitted from using AI tools to generate content
units.frag_start: Outside of those circumstances, you are
units.policy: Outside circumstances where students are asked to use AI tools, students are not permitted to use AI tools to generate content (text, video, audio, images, etc.) that will end up in any course work submitted in the course.

units.why: 'you will be asked to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to explore how they can be used' says some activities require AI use (P44, teaching AI use as a skill).
units.anchor: you will be asked to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to explore
units.policy: There are some situations and contexts in the course where students will be asked to use AI tools to explore how they can be used.

units.why: 'You are discouraged from using generative AI tools except when instructed to do so' discourages without a flat ban (P03).
units.anchor: You are discouraged from using generative AI tools
units.policy: Students are discouraged from using generative AI tools except when instructed to do so.

units.why: 'Please contact me if you are unsure or have questions before using AI tools for any assignment' is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: Please contact me if you are unsure or have questions
units.policy: Students who are unsure or have questions should contact the instructor before using AI tools for any assignment.

units.why: 'you must indicate what part of the assignment was written by the AI tool and what was written by you' requires marking the AI-produced portions (P27 over generic P24 because it marks where AI content sits).
units.anchor: you must indicate what part of the assignment was written by the AI tool
units.frag_start: If generative AI tools are permitted
units.policy: If generative AI tools are permitted, students must indicate what part of the assignment was written by the AI tool and what was written by them.

units.why: 'You may also be asked to explain how you personally used these tools' is a request to account for AI use (P34, explaining work).
units.anchor: You may also be asked to explain how you personally used these tools
units.frag_start: You may also be asked to
units.policy: Students may be asked to explain how they personally used AI tools to complete the assignment.

units.why: 'Individual assignments permitting AI tools will provide more specific guidance' makes the rule assignment-specific (P04).
units.anchor: Individual assignments permitting AI tools will provide more specific guidance
units.frag_end: to what extent, they can be used
units.policy: Individual assignments permitting AI tools will provide more specific guidance about how, and to what extent, they can be used.

units.why: 'regardless of whether AI use is permitted, must be completed in ways that avoid violation of the university’s policies on academic integrity and AI use' ties all work to integrity rules (P36).
units.anchor: must be completed in ways that avoid violation of the university’s policies
units.frag_start: All assignments in this course, regardless
units.policy: All assignments in the course, regardless of whether AI use is permitted, must be completed in ways that avoid violation of the university's policies on academic integrity and AI use.

units.why: 'please reach out to me for a conversation before submitting your work' repeats the ask-first expectation (P10); coded once here, the same sentence recurs in Option 2.
units.anchor: please reach out to me for a conversation
units.frag_start: If you have any questions about how
units.policy: Students with questions about how and when it is appropriate to use AI tools should reach out to the instructor for a conversation before submitting work.

units.why: 'AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking' explains why AI use is limited, keeping students as thinkers (P32).
units.anchor: AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking
units.frag_start: While we recognize that there are
units.policy: AI programs are not a replacement for human creativity, originality, and critical thinking.

units.why: 'The purpose of assignments in this course is for you to demonstrate your writing, critical thinking, and analytical skills' gives a rationale for doing the work oneself (P41).
units.anchor: The purpose of assignments in this course is for you to demonstrate
units.policy: The purpose of assignments in the course is for students to demonstrate their writing, critical thinking, and analytical skills while growing as communicators, thinkers, and scholars.

units.why: 'I may sometimes incorporate the use of generative AI tools like ChatGPT into your lessons and assignments' states the instructor builds AI into course work (P44).
units.anchor: I may sometimes incorporate the use of generative AI tools like ChatGPT
units.frag_end: as a valuable tool for learning
units.policy: The instructor may sometimes incorporate generative AI tools like ChatGPT into lessons and assignments, in which AI is used as a valuable tool for learning.

units.why: 'in instances where you are not specifically told to use generative AI, I ask you to ... write without using these tools' sets no AI unless told (P06 fits better than P01 because it is conditioned on being instructed).
units.anchor: in instances where you are not specifically told to use generative AI
units.frag_start: However, in instances where you are
units.policy: In instances where students are not specifically told to use generative AI, they are asked to write without using these tools.

units.why: 'work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original' requires that submitted work be the student's own (P29).
units.anchor: work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original
units.frag_start: In all academic work, the ideas
units.policy: In all academic work, work that is presented as original must be, in fact, original.

units.why: 'Using an AI-content generator ... without proper citation of source(s) or permission is a form of academic dishonesty' classifies it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: is a form of academic dishonesty
units.policy: Using an AI-content generator (such as ChatGPT) to complete coursework without proper citation of source(s) or permission is a form of academic dishonesty.

units.why: 'If you are unsure about whether something may be in violation ... please reach out to me' is an ask-first instruction (P10).
units.anchor: If you are unsure about whether something may be in violation
units.frag_start: If you are unsure about whether
units.policy: Students who are unsure whether something may violate university policies on academic integrity and AI use should reach out to the instructor before submitting work.

units.why: 'Faculty, students, and administrative staff all share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness' states shared responsibility as a framework principle (P56).
units.anchor: all share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness
units.policy: Faculty, students, and administrative staff all share the responsibility of ensuring the honesty and fairness of the intellectual environment at Chapman University.

units.why: The no-use statement says use of generative models 'such as ChatGPT, Haptic and Microsoft Copilot ... is not permitted', a default ban (P01).
units.anchor: is not permitted
units.frag_start: the use of generative models of artificial
units.policy: The use of generative models of artificial intelligence such as ChatGPT, Haptic and Microsoft Copilot (among others) is not permitted.

units.why: 'paraphrasing tools such as Spinbot and Wordtune are also prohibited' bans a class of writing tools (P18, prose-specific rule).
units.anchor: paraphrasing tools such as Spinbot and Wordtune are also prohibited
units.policy: Paraphrasing tools such as Spinbot and Wordtune are also prohibited.

units.why: 'you may use university approved programs such as Grammarly to check for spelling and grammar errors' permits vetted tools for prose checks (P18 over P50 since the point is the grammar use).
units.anchor: you may use university approved programs such as Grammarly
units.frag_start: While you may use university approved
units.policy: Students may use university approved programs such as Grammarly to check for spelling and grammar errors.

units.why: 'it is fundamental that all text be produced solely by you' states submitted text must come from the student, not AI (P19).
units.anchor: all text be produced solely by you
units.frag_start: it is fundamental that all text
units.policy: All text must be produced solely by the student.

units.why: 'It is essential that all work turned in for this class represents your personal analytical and critical thinking skills' states that students remain the thinkers (P32).
units.anchor: represents your personal analytical and critical thinking skills
units.frag_start: It is essential that all work
units.policy: All work turned in for the class must represent the student's personal analytical and critical thinking skills.

units.why: 'If you use a program such as Google Translate or ChatGPT to help with translation, speak with me' requires consultation for translation use (P18, prose and translation tools).
units.anchor: speak with me to discuss implications and limitations
units.frag_start: If you use a program such as
units.policy: If a student uses a program such as Google Translate or ChatGPT to help with translation, the student speaks with the instructor to discuss implications and limitations.

units.why: 'I will check the various services that can detect this. If those services confirm my suspicion, I will call you in for a conference' describes using detectors to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: I will check the various services that can detect this
units.frag_start: If I suspect that your response
units.frag_end: call you in for a conference
units.policy: If the instructor suspects a response was produced by an LLM, the instructor checks services that can detect this and, if confirmed, calls the student in for a conference.

units.why: 'If you are in doubt about whether a specific form of aid is allowed, please speak directly with me' is an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: If you are in doubt about whether a specific form of aid is allowed
units.frag_start: If you are in doubt about
units.policy: Students in doubt about whether a specific form of aid is allowed should speak directly with the instructor.

units.why: The caution says a 'No Use' position 'would be more likely to increase academic integrity violations without a clear, direct benefit', steering instructors away from a blanket ban (P04: instructors decide but are steered).
units.anchor: more likely to increase academic integrity violations without a clear, direct benefit
units.frag_start: You may feel tempted, especially at
units.policy: The task force cautions instructors against selecting a 'No Use of AI Permitted' syllabus statement because it would be more likely to increase academic integrity violations without a clear, direct benefit.

units.why: 'students have already adapted AI tools into their learning, studying, and writing methods' gives the factual reason against a ban (P44, AI-rich life and work).
units.anchor: students have already adapted AI tools into their learning, studying, and writing methods
units.frag_start: Whether we like it or not,
units.frag_end: that we likely do not comprehend
units.policy: AI tools are already in heavy use in almost every context of modern life, and students have already adapted AI tools into their learning, studying, and writing methods.

units.why: The task force asks instructors to 'think carefully about whether you are certain that these tools will negatively affect students’ ability to accomplish the learning outcomes' before banning, guidance on how to decide (P04).
units.anchor: think carefully about whether you are certain that these tools will negatively affect
units.frag_start: we ask that you instead think carefully
units.frag_end: essential for college students to learn
units.policy: Before adopting a 'no AI' position, instructors should think carefully about whether AI tools will negatively affect students' ability to accomplish course learning outcomes and whether they might hinder or assist attainment of secondary and soft skills.

units.why: 'please consider speaking with a member of our Task Force or reading some of the Teaching & Learning resources' routes instructors to support (P63).
units.anchor: please consider speaking with a member of our Task Force
units.frag_start: Before taking such a decision, please
units.frag_end: resources we have collected around this issue
units.policy: Before deciding on a 'no use' position, instructors should consider speaking with a member of the Task Force or reading the Teaching & Learning resources collected on the issue.

units.why: The organization section directs questions to 'the Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning and/or any member of this task force' (P63).
units.anchor: reach out to the Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning
units.frag_start: Should you have questions or need
units.frag_end: any member of this task force
units.policy: Instructors with questions or needing more guidance should reach out to the Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning and/or any member of the task force.

units.why: The resources entry says there 'are no AI-proof assessments' but offers 'generative AI-resistant' assignment strategies as starting points, which relates to assessment redesign (P35).
units.anchor: There are no “AI-proof” assessments
units.frag_start: While some educators are excited about
units.policy: The guide links strategies for creating generative AI-resistant assessments, noting that there are no AI-proof assessments, as starting points for authentic assignments requiring original and critical thinking.

documents.title: Academic Integrity: Important Guidelines for Students (2025)
documents.summary: Student-facing process guide for Chapman's Academic Integrity Committee covering meetings, appeals and hearings. AI appears only in the definition of plagiarism and in a line telling students to follow instructor guidelines on AI.
documents.stance_why: The only AI content is that plagiarism includes presenting an 'artificial intelligence' work as one's own and that students must 'adhere to instructor guidelines ... including ... use of artificial intelligence'; the document sets no AI stance and defers to instructors.

units.why: Plagiarism is defined as 'presenting the words, research findings or ideas of another person (or an artificial intelligence) as your own', which defines AI-presented-as-own as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: presenting the words, research findings or ideas of another person (or
units.frag_end: an artificial intelligence) as your own
units.policy: Plagiarism is presenting the words, research findings or ideas of another person (or an artificial intelligence) as your own, a form of academic dishonesty.

units.why: The 'unauthorized assistance, information or study aids' item is not AI-specific, but unauthorized aids include AI where instructors do not allow it; it fits P36 as a category of misconduct.
units.anchor: Cheating through the use of unauthorized assistance
units.policy: Cheating through the use of unauthorized assistance is the use of unauthorized assistance, information or study aids on any academic exercise.

units.why: Students 'should be aware and adhere to instructor guidelines for projects, papers and exam situations including ... use of artificial intelligence', deferring AI rules to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: adhere to instructor guidelines for projects, papers and exam situations
units.frag_start: Students should be aware and adhere
units.policy: Students should be aware of and adhere to instructor guidelines for projects, papers and exam situations, including appropriate citations and/or use of artificial intelligence.

units.why: 'The student will be given the opportunity to respond and ... to submit evidence refuting the allegation' is the right to respond in integrity cases; not AI-specific but it covers AI misuse allegations (P64).
units.anchor: The student will be given the opportunity to respond
units.frag_start: In the meeting, the instructor will
units.policy: In the meeting, the instructor presents the student with the allegation and all supporting evidence, and the student is given the opportunity to respond and, if they wish, to submit evidence refuting the allegation.

units.why: The instructor decides on a 'more likely than not' basis; a general process that applies to AI plagiarism, so P36 as it routes misuse through the integrity process (no specific penalty named, so not P37).
units.anchor: it is more likely than not that the student has violated
units.frag_start: the instructor determines if it is
units.policy: At the conclusion of the meeting, the instructor determines if it is more likely than not that the student has violated the Academic Integrity Policy.

units.why: Students 'retain the right to appeal' to the AIC and then the Provost, a due-process right in integrity cases that includes AI allegations (P64).
units.anchor: Students retain the right to appeal
units.policy: Students retain the right to appeal whether or not the instructor has submitted the case to the AIC.

units.why: Appeals may rest on new evidence, procedural error, an inappropriate sanction, or insufficient facts; a fairness safeguard in integrity cases (P64).
units.anchor: There was a substantive procedural error made in charging the student.
units.frag_start: New evidence not available at the
units.frag_end: a violation of the policy occurred
units.policy: Appeals must demonstrate at least one criterion: new evidence, substantive procedural error in charging, inappropriate sanction, or facts insufficient to establish a violation.

units.why: The AIC reviews a second violation 'regardless of whether the student decides to appeal', escalation by offense count that applies to all integrity violations (P37 considered; no concrete penalty is named, so P36).
units.anchor: the AIC will review the case regardless of whether the student decides to appeal
units.frag_start: If the violation represents a second violation
units.policy: If the violation represents a second violation of the Academic Integrity Policy, the AIC will review the case regardless of whether the student decides to appeal.

units.why: 'The standard of proof applied by the AIC is preponderance of the evidence' sets how integrity cases, including AI cases, are decided (P64: fairness and transparency).
units.anchor: The standard of proof applied by the AIC is preponderance of the evidence
units.frag_start: The standard of proof applied by

units.policy: The standard of proof applied by the AIC is preponderance of the evidence, i.e. whether it is more likely than not that the student violated the Academic Integrity Policy.
